content: This systematic review represents the second update on the topic of pharmacotherapy for hyperuricaemia in hypertensive patients. Hypertension is a significant global public health issue, affecting approximately one-fourth of the adult population worldwide. Epidemiological and experimental evidence suggests a potential association between hyperuricaemia and hypertension. Hyperuricaemia is present in 25% to 40% of individuals with untreated hypertension, whereas its prevalence is much lower in normotensive individuals or the general population. However, it remains unclear whether reducing serum uric acid (UA) levels can effectively lower blood pressure (BP). The objective of this review was to evaluate whether UA-lowering agents reduce BP in individuals with primary hypertension or prehypertension, compared to placebo. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hypertension Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, and LILACS, up to May 2020. The search was unrestricted by language or date. Authors of relevant studies were also contacted for additional published or unpublished data. To be included in the review, studies had to meet specific criteria: they needed to be randomised or quasi-randomised trials with at least one group receiving a UA-lowering agent and another receiving placebo. The trials could be double-blind, single-blind, or open-label, with either a parallel or cross-over design. Cross-over trials required a washout period of at least two weeks. The minimum treatment duration was four weeks. Participants had to have essential hypertension or prehypertension with hyperuricaemia, defined as serum UA levels exceeding 6 mg/dL in women, 7 mg/dL in men, and 5.5 mg/dL in children or adolescents. Outcome measures included changes in 24-hour ambulatory systolic or diastolic BP, or clinic-measured systolic or diastolic BP. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two review authors, who resolved disagreements through discussion. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. In this updated review, 722 records were screened, and 26 full-text reports were evaluated. No new studies were added, and no ongoing studies were identified. Ultimately, three randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving 211 participants with hypertension or prehypertension and hyperuricaemia were included. The evidence from these RCTs was of low certainty. The results regarding the effect of UA-lowering drugs on 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP (mean difference [MD] -6.2 mmHg, 95% confidence interval [CI] -12.8 to 0.5) and diastolic BP (MD -3.9 mmHg, 95% CI -9.2 to 1.4) were inconclusive. Similarly, low-certainty evidence from two RCTs suggested that UA-lowering drugs reduced clinic-measured systolic BP (MD -8.43 mmHg, 95% CI -15.24 to -1.62), but the results for clinic-measured diastolic BP were inconclusive (MD -6.45 mmHg, 95% CI -13.60 to 0.70). High-certainty evidence from three RCTs demonstrated that UA-lowering drugs effectively reduced serum UA levels by 3.1 mg/dL (95% CI 2.4 to 3.8). However, low-certainty evidence from three RCTs showed inconclusive results regarding the occurrence of adverse events between participants receiving UA-lowering drugs and those receiving placebo (risk ratio [RR] 1.86, 95% CI 0.43 to 8.10). In conclusion, the current evidence from RCTs is insufficient to determine whether UA-lowering therapy effectively reduces BP in individuals with hypertension or prehypertension. Further high-quality studies are needed to address this question.
